title: Hong Kong rainfall
deck: Daily rainfall at the Hong Kong Observatory, 1884 to 2025. Each year becomes six diagnostics: its wettest day, how rare that day is, how concentrated the rain was, its day-to-day spread, how often it rained, and its total against the previous 30 years. A PCA learns what a typical year looks like and scores how badly each year fits it, the anomaly, and finds two factors in the same numbers: intensity and wetness. Arousal is how intense and how surprising the year was. Valence falls with how far the year departs from a normal one, wetter, drier or more intense, and with how surprising it was. Both are ranks within this record: a hypothesis about affect, not yet tested with viewers.
steps: Daily rainfall at the Hong Kong Observatory, 1884 to 2025, as an ECG: every spike is a real day's rain, and the trace moves through the years as the heart beats, one year per beat. Click it to jump to a year.

Each year is summarised by six numbers. Like an ECG, each beat is one year, placed at the date of its wettest day; its height is the chosen diagnostic, in standard deviations from typical, up or down.
An unsupervised model learns what a typical year looks like. Each beat's height and colour is how badly that year fits it, from typical to most unusual, scaled within this record.
method: PCA with 2 components, fitted on the complete years of this record.

features.label: Peak daily rainfall
features.desc: The wettest single day of the year.

features.label: Day-to-day spread
features.desc: How much daily rainfall varies within the year.

features.label: Wet-day frequency
features.desc: Share of days with at least 0.1 mm.

features.label: Total vs recent norm
features.desc: The year's total against the mean of the 30 years before it (0 = normal, +0.5 = half again as much).

features.label: Rarity of the peak
features.desc: log10 of the peak's fitted return period in years: how rarely a day that wet comes round.

features.label: Peak concentration
features.desc: Share of the year's rain that fell on the peak day.

limits: The model flags unusual combinations of features, not extremes. 1931 is among the top-scoring years with a peak of only 91 mm, while 1926, which holds the largest single day (534 mm), scores 0.78 and 2023 scores 0.45, on a scale where 1 is the most unusual year of the record. The 1963 drought scores 0.05.

Valence and arousal (the corner map) are relative to this record: each year is placed against its 134 fitted years. They combine two PCA factors learned from the data, intensity and wetness, with the anomaly score, and agree with it (arousal r = +0.65, valence r = -0.64). They pass 7 of 8 consistency checks fixed in advance; valence and arousal share about half their variance (r = -0.71). No viewers rated anything, so this is a hypothesis about affect, not a measurement.
There are no data for 1940–1946, so the record has 135 years rather than 142. 2025 is a partial year (the data end in January): it is scored by the fitted model and never shaped it.
Years with missing days are totalled and summarised over the days that exist (n_days is between 268 and 299 for 55 of the 135 years).
Nothing here has been tested with viewers. A high score means the year was unusual for this record, not that a person would feel it so.
